pos: n. (proper name; a son of Ram, of the house of Jerahmeel in Judah)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eqer, root or offshoot, from 'aqar, to pluck up by the roots; the noun means a transplanted stock.
biblical_def: Eker is a man of Judah in the line of Jerahmeel: “And the sons of Ram the firstborn of Jerahmeel were, Maaz, and Jamin, and Eker” (1 Chronicles 2:27). Jerahmeel was the firstborn of Hezron, son of Pharez, son of Judah, and his house was one of the three great branches of Hezron, the others being Ram, whose line led to David, and Chelubai, or Caleb. This Ram is a different man from David's ancestor: he is the firstborn of Jerahmeel, “Ram the firstborn, and Bunah, and Oren, and Ozem, and Ahijah” (1 Chronicles 2:25). Eker's name means a root or offshoot, the word used in Leviticus of a stranger's stock transplanted into Israel. Nothing else is known of him. The Chronicler preserved the Jerahmeelite lines, which seldom appear elsewhere in Scripture, because every branch of Judah had its place in the tribe from which the King would come.

corruption_summary: The lesser branches of a genealogy are counted as dead wood; the Chronicler kept the Jerahmeelite line as part of Judah's living tree.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern readers often look in genealogies only for the famous line and treat the rest as scaffolding. The Chronicler spent a whole section on Jerahmeel's house, a branch of Judah that produced no king.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God counts every branch of His people. The root of Jesse bore the King, and the other roots of Judah are written in the same book.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Judah, father of the men of Rechah)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eshton, perhaps uxorious or restful; the meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Eshton is a man of Judah whose sons founded a cluster of settlements: “And Chelub the brother of Shuah begat Mehir, which was the father of Eshton. And Eshton begat Bethrapha, and Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Irnahash. These are the men of Rechah” (1 Chronicles 4:11-12). Several of his descendants' names are place-names: Bethrapha is a house, Irnahash a city, and the margin renders Irnahash “the city of Nahash”. In the Chronicler's usage to beget a place is to found or settle it, and Eshton's line established villages in the hill country of Judah whose very locations are now lost. “These are the men of Rechah” closes the paragraph like a signature, though Rechah itself is otherwise unknown. Eshton is one of those quiet founders whose work outlived his memory, recorded so that the towns of Judah would know whose sons they were.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Ashur of Tekoa by Helah)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ethnan, gift or hire, from 'ethnan, a gift, wage, especially a harlot's hire.
biblical_def: Ethnan is the third son of Helah, wife of Ashur the father of Tekoa: “And the sons of Helah were, Zereth, and Jezoar, and Ethnan” (1 Chronicles 4:7). His father Ashur had two wives, “Helah and Naarah” (1 Chronicles 4:5), and by Naarah four more sons, so that the house of Tekoa's founder was a divided one. Ethnan's name is the Hebrew word for a gift or wage, a word the prophets use bitterly of the harlot's hire: Hosea says Israel loved a reward upon every cornfloor, and Micah that Samaria's images were gathered of the hire of an harlot. Why a son of Judah would bear that name is not told. Its presence in a genealogy is one of the small reminders that the names in these lists are real names given by real parents, sometimes for reasons we cannot recover, and that God kept the record of the house of Tekoa as faithfully as of the house of David.

corruption_summary: Gifts are treated as morally neutral; the Hebrew word in Ethnan's name is the prophets' word for the hire of spiritual harlotry.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern thinking assumes that what one receives is simply one's due. The prophets distinguished sharply between God's gifts and the wages of idolatry, and they used this very word for the latter.

The principle to recover is that every good gift is from above. The wages Israel took from its idols were a harlot's hire, and the believer must ask of every gain whether it came from God or from a compromise with His rivals.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Ashur of Tekoa by Naarah; properly, the Ahashtarite)
etymology: Hebrew Ha'achashtari, the Ahashtarite, with the article, perhaps from Persian achashteran, royal, a word used of the king's mules in Esther.
biblical_def: Haahashtari is the last of the four sons Naarah bore to Ashur the father of Tekoa: “And Naarah bare him Ahuzam, and Hepher, and Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah” (1 Chronicles 4:6). The name carries the Hebrew article, the Ahashtarite, which suggests a clan or family name rather than a personal one, perhaps attached to a son whose descendants formed a distinct group. Its form is unusual in a Hebrew genealogy; some have linked it to a Persian word for royal service that appears in Esther of the king's swift mules. Whatever its origin, the Chronicler keeps it in the line of Tekoa beside the sons of Helah, Zereth, Jezoar, and Ethnan. Tekoa later gave Israel a wise woman whom Joab used to bring Absalom home and a herdsman named Amos whom God took from following the flock. The lesser names of its founding family stand behind both.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Caleb, father of Beth-gader)
etymology: Hebrew Chareph, plucking or reproachful, from charaph, to reproach, or to pluck in harvest.
biblical_def: Hareph is one of the sons of Caleb the son of Hur who founded towns in Judah: “These were the sons of Caleb the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah; Shobal the father of Kirjathjearim, Salma the father of Bethlehem, Hareph the father of Bethgader” (1 Chronicles 2:50-51). To be called the father of a town is to be its founder or chief. Hareph's brothers founded Kirjath-jearim, where the ark rested twenty years, and Bethlehem, the city of David and of Christ. His own town, Beth-gader, the house of the wall, is barely mentioned elsewhere; it may be the Geder whose king Joshua smote. The verse sets three brothers side by side, and two of their towns became famous while the third stayed obscure. Hareph's name comes from a root meaning to reproach; it is a small reminder that in the providence of God the obscure brother is as surely recorded as the founder of Bethlehem.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Aharhel, a head of families in Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Harum, exalted or high, from rum, to be high.
biblical_def: Harum is named once, in a terse verse of Judah's genealogy: “And Coz begat Anub, and Zobebah, and the families of Aharhel the son of Harum” (1 Chronicles 4:8). The structure is unusual: Coz is said to beget not only sons but families, and among them the families of Aharhel, whose father was Harum. Harum was evidently the head of a house distinct enough to be named in its own right, connected by marriage or adoption to the line of Coz. The verse sits just before the most famous name in this part of Chronicles. “And Jabez was more honourable than his brethren” (1 Chronicles 4:9), and he prayed, “Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast”, and God granted his request. Harum, the exalted, is named in passing on the way to that prayer. The Chronicler's lists are not merely tables; they are the soil out of which such prayers grew.

corruption_paragraphs: Popular devotional writing has turned the prayer of Jabez into a technique for enlargement. In its setting it is the prayer of one honourable man among the families of Judah, Harum's among them, asking that God's hand be with him and keep him from evil.
The principle to recover is that prayer is dependence, not leverage. Jabez asked for blessing and for protection from sin, and God granted what He was pleased to grant.

pos: n. (proper name; a town of Judah founded by Ezer, home of Sibbechai the Hushathite)
biblical_def: Hushah appears in Judah's genealogy as the foundation of Ezer, a son of Hur: “And Penuel the father of Gedor, and Ezer the father of Hushah. These are the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah, the father of Bethlehem” (1 Chronicles 4:4). As often in Chronicles, the father of a town is its founder, and Hushah is both a person-name and a place. Its most famous son was Sibbechai the Hushathite, one of David's mighty men, who at Gob “slew Saph, which was of the sons of the giant” (2 Samuel 21:18), and who later commanded the eighth monthly course of twenty-four thousand men (1 Chronicles 27:11). A village founded by a grandson of Hur near Bethlehem produced a giant-killer for David's army. The connections are typical of these genealogies: an obscure name in chapter 4 explains where a hero in another book came from.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture interprets Scripture. The lists in Chronicles give roots to the deeds recorded in Samuel, and both together give a coherent history.

pos: n. (proper name; a Simeonite, son of Mishma)
etymology: Hebrew Chammu'el, wrath of God or warmth of God, from chamam, to be hot, and 'el, God.
biblical_def: Hamuel is a man of Simeon: “And the sons of Mishma; Hamuel his son, Zacchur his son, Shimei his son” (1 Chronicles 4:26). His line leads to Shimei, who “had sixteen sons and six daughters; but his brethren had not many children, neither did all their family multiply, like to the children of Judah” (1 Chronicles 4:27). The comparison is pointed. Simeon had been under a curse since Jacob's last words: “Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7), spoken of Simeon and Levi for the massacre at Shechem. Simeon's inheritance was swallowed within Judah's, “within the inheritance of the children of Judah” (Joshua 19:1), and the tribe dwindled. Hamuel's name, wrath of God, sits strikingly in a tribe whose history bore the weight of a father's curse on anger.

corruption_summary: Anger is excused as passion for justice; Jacob cursed Simeon's cruel wrath, and the tribe bore the consequence for generations.
corruption_paragraphs: Simeon and Levi's slaughter at Shechem is sometimes defended as righteous anger over their sister. Jacob did not defend it; he cursed it on his deathbed, and Simeon's scattered, diminished history followed.

The principle to recover is that the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God. Levi's scattering was turned to blessing through the priesthood; Simeon's became absorption into Judah. Grace can redeem a curse, but anger leaves its mark.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Othniel the judge)
etymology: Hebrew Chathath, terror or dismay, from chathath, to be shattered, dismayed.
biblical_def: Hathath is the son of Othniel, the first of Israel's judges: “And the sons of Kenaz; Othniel, and Seraiah: and the sons of Othniel; Hathath” (1 Chronicles 4:13). Othniel had taken Kirjath-sepher and received Achsah, Caleb's daughter, as his wife, and when Israel served Chushan-rishathaim eight years, “the LORD raised up a deliverer to the children of Israel, who delivered them, even Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother” (Judges 3:9). Hathath was born into that house, the grandson of Caleb's brother and the son of Caleb's daughter. His name means terror or dismay, perhaps given in the years of oppression or as a mark of what his father would be to Israel's enemies. The next verse turns to Seraiah's son Joab, “the father of the valley of Charashim; for they were craftsmen” (1 Chronicles 4:14), so that the house of Kenaz produced both a deliverer and a settlement of skilled workmen.

pos: n. (proper name; a son and a grandson of Caleb by his concubine Ephah)
biblical_def: Gazez is named twice in one verse of Caleb's genealogy: “And Ephah, Caleb's concubine, bare Haran, and Moza, and Gazez: and Haran begat Gazez” (1 Chronicles 2:46). So there were two men of the name, an uncle and a nephew, the second perhaps named for the first. Caleb here is Caleb the son of Hezron, “Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel” (1 Chronicles 2:42), whose household the Chronicler traces in detail with his wives Azubah and Jerioth and Ephrath and his concubines Ephah and Maachah. Gazez's name means shearer, a fitting name in the sheep country of the Judean hills, where shearing was the great festival of the year. The record of the concubines' sons is part of the Chronicler's thoroughness: the lines that did not lead to the throne were kept with the same care as the line that did.

corruption_summary: The concubines' children are thought beneath record; the Chronicler names them with care beside the heirs.
corruption_paragraphs: In many ancient records the children of secondary wives disappear. The Chronicler names Ephah and her sons, and even repeats the name Gazez for the grandson, as carefully as he traces the main line.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God sees the children of irregular households. The law did not approve concubinage, but the record does not erase the children it produced.
roots_summary: Hebrew Gazez, shearer; a son and a grandson of Caleb by his concubine Ephah.
roots_lines: Hebrew Gazez, from gazaz, to shear.
A son of Caleb by Ephah his concubine (1 Chronicles 2:46).
A second Gazez was the son of Haran, Caleb's son.
Caleb here is the son of Hezron, brother of Jerahmeel.
Of the sheep country of Judah.
